content: The transdermal system containing norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol is a hormonal contraceptive approved by the FDA for the prevention of pregnancy. It is important to note that this medication carries a Black Box Warning due to associated risks. Common Adverse Reactions The most frequently reported adverse effects include breast symptoms, nausea and vomiting, headaches, application site reactions, abdominal pain, dysmenorrhea, vaginal bleeding, menstrual disorders, and mood or anxiety disorders. Indications and Dosage This contraceptive is indicated for women who choose to use a transdermal patch as their method of contraception. However, its effectiveness may be reduced in women weighing 198 pounds (90 kg) or more. To maximize contraceptive efficacy, the patch must be used exactly as directed. A 28-day cycle is followed, with a new patch applied weekly for three weeks, followed by a patch-free week during which withdrawal bleeding is expected. Each new patch should be applied on the same day of the week, known as the Patch Change Day. Only one patch should be worn at a time, and it should not be cut, damaged, or altered, as this may compromise its effectiveness. Starting the Patch Women can begin using the patch in one of two ways: 1. First Day Start: Apply the first patch within the first 24 hours of the menstrual period. 2. Sunday Start: Apply the first patch on the first Sunday after the menstrual period begins. A non-hormonal backup method (e.g., condoms with spermicide) is required for the first 7 days of the initial cycle unless the period starts on a Sunday, in which case no backup is needed. When switching from oral contraceptives or vaginal rings, the first patch should be applied on the day the next pill or ring would have been started. If the patch is applied more than a week after stopping the previous method, a backup contraceptive method should be used for the first 7 days. Use After Childbirth, Abortion, or Miscarriage After childbirth, women who are not breastfeeding should wait at least 4 weeks before starting the patch due to an increased risk of thromboembolism. After a first-trimester abortion or miscarriage, the patch can be started immediately without the need for additional contraception. If not started within 5 days, follow the instructions for first-time users and use a backup method in the interim. After a second-trimester abortion or miscarriage, wait at least 4 weeks before starting the patch due to thromboembolic risk. Contraindications The patch should not be prescribed to women with the following conditions: High risk of arterial or venous thrombotic diseases (e.g., smokers over 35, history of deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, inherited or acquired hypercoagulopathies, cerebrovascular or coronary artery disease, uncontrolled hypertension, diabetes with vascular disease, or migraines with aura). Liver disease or tumors. Unexplained abnormal uterine bleeding. Pregnancy or known estrogenor progestin-sensitive cancers (e.g., breast cancer). Warnings Thromboembolic Disorders: Discontinue use if a thrombotic event occurs or if there is unexplained vision loss, proptosis, diplopia, papilledema, or retinal vascular lesions. Evaluate for retinal vein thrombosis immediately. Surgery and Immobility: Stop the patch at least 4 weeks before and 2 weeks after major surgery or prolonged immobilization. Postpartum Use: Do not start earlier than 4 weeks postpartum in non-breastfeeding women due to increased thromboembolic risk. Vascular Risks: Combination hormonal contraceptives (CHCs) increase the risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE) and arterial thrombosis, particularly in women with additional risk factors such as smoking, obesity, or a family history of VTE. Adverse Reactions and Monitoring Common adverse reactions include irregular uterine bleeding, nausea, breast tenderness, and headaches. Women using CHCs should have an annual visit with their healthcare provider for blood pressure monitoring and other indicated health checks. Special Considerations Liver Disease: Do not use in women with acute or chronic liver disease. Discontinue if jaundice develops. Gallbladder Disease: CHCs may increase the risk of gallbladder disease or worsen pre-existing conditions. Carbohydrate and Lipid Metabolism: Monitor women with prediabetes or diabetes, as CHCs may decrease glucose tolerance. Consider alternative contraception for women with uncontrolled dyslipidemia. Headaches: Evaluate new, recurrent, or severe headaches and discontinue the patch if indicated. Bleeding Irregularities: Investigate unscheduled bleeding to rule out malignancy or pregnancy. Time or switching to another contraceptive may resolve the issue. Amenorrhea: Rule out pregnancy if amenorrhea occurs, especially if the dosing schedule was not followed. Use During Pregnancy Discontinue the patch if pregnancy is confirmed. Extensive studies have shown no increased risk of birth defects with prior CHC use. Depression Carefully monitor women with a history of depression and discontinue the patch if depression recurs to a serious degree. Cancer Risks The patch is contraindicated in women with current or past breast cancer. Some studies suggest an association between CHC use and cervical cancer, but this may be influenced by other factors such as sexual behavior. Binding Globulins The estrogen component may increase serum concentrations of binding globulins, potentially requiring adjustments in thyroid hormone or cortisol therapy. Hereditary Angioedema Exogenous estrogens may exacerbate symptoms of hereditary angioedema. Chloasma Women prone to chloasma should avoid sun or ultraviolet exposure while using the patch. This information highlights the importance of careful patient selection, monitoring, and adherence to prescribed usage to minimize risks and maximize the benefits of norelgestromin and ethinyl estradiol transdermal systems.
